pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Grouping Species Using DNA / Cladistics (ages 13–14): organisms are classified by shared DERIVED characters (not overall similarity); phylogenetic trees are built from molecular data (DNA sequence alignment) and calibrated with the molecular clock; birds are a group WITHIN dinosaurs; convergent vs parallel evolution; horizontal gene transfer makes the 'tree' of life partly a web; classifications keep changing as new data arrive.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): 'the variation between species and between individuals', heredity and the genome (DNA), and classification; extends the traditional Linnaean grouping into evidence-based, evolutionary classification.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-2/MS-LS4-3 (anatomical and embryological/DNA similarities as evidence of evolutionary relationships); HS-LS4-1 horizon (evidence for common ancestry).
• Operational details: the key conceptual shift is grouping by SHARED DERIVED characters (synapomorphies) and common ancestry, not by looking alike — so a crocodile is more closely related to a bird than to a lizard, and 'reptiles' (excluding birds) is not a true clade. Teach how molecular data (aligning DNA/protein sequences; counting differences; molecular clock) build and date trees, and why more data revises classifications. Distinguish convergent evolution (unrelated lineages, similar traits from similar pressures — dolphin vs shark) from shared ancestry, and note horizontal gene transfer webbing the tree (esp. microbes). Read a cladogram: nodes = common ancestors, branching = shared-ancestry hypotheses.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~13): read a simple cladogram — identify which species share the most recent common ancestor. B (transitional, ~13–14): explain why grouping by shared derived characters/DNA can override grouping by resemblance (birds within dinosaurs; convergence misleads). C (formal, ~14): explain how molecular data build/date trees, why classifications change with new evidence, and how horizontal gene transfer complicates the tree.
bestPractices: Teach reading cladograms explicitly (nodes as common ancestors, branch points as shared-derived-character hypotheses) before building them — tree literacy is a documented stumbling block.

Confront convergence head-on: give look-alike but distantly related pairs (dolphin/shark, bird wing/bat wing/insect wing) so pupils learn resemblance can mislead and shared DERIVED characters/DNA arbitrate.
Use real reclassifications (birds nested within dinosaurs; whales within artiodactyls near hippos) to show classification as evidence-driven and revisable, not arbitrary or fixed.
Introduce molecular comparison concretely — more sequence differences ≈ longer since common ancestor — then add the molecular-clock caveat that rates vary, so trees are hypotheses.
keyRepresentations: A cladogram with labelled nodes (common ancestors) and synapomorphies marked on branches.
A DNA sequence-alignment panel where counting differences between species orders their relatedness.
A convergence vs homology contrast: dolphin/shark body shape (convergent) beside genuinely homologous limbs.
A 'tree becoming a web' diagram showing horizontal gene transfer links between branches (microbes).
A before/after classification showing birds moved inside the dinosaur clade.
commonMisconceptions: 'Things that look alike are most closely related' — convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages; shared derived characters/DNA are the evidence.
'Higher/more advanced species evolved FROM the living species next to them on the tree' — tips are all modern; they share common ANCESTORS at the nodes, they don't descend from each other.
'Birds and dinosaurs are separate groups' — birds are a lineage within (theropod) dinosaurs.
'Classification is arbitrary or fixed forever' — it is an evidence-based hypothesis that changes as new (esp. molecular) data emerge.
'Evolution is always a branching tree' — horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) makes parts of the tree of life a web.
'The molecular clock is exact' — mutation rates vary across lineages/genes, so molecular dates carry uncertainty.

learn.summary: Cladistics for ages 13–14: group organisms by shared DERIVED characters (synapomorphies) and common ancestry, not by overall resemblance. Learners read and build phylogenetic trees from molecular data (DNA sequence alignment, counting differences), confront convergent evolution as a misleading resemblance, see that classification is an evidence-driven hypothesis that revises with new data (birds nested within dinosaurs; whales near hippos/artiodactyls), and meet horizontal gene transfer webbing the tree, plus the molecular clock with its rate-variation uncertainty.

activities.title: Build and revise a tree from character and DNA data
feedback: If a learner keeps a look-alike species on a resemblance-based branch after DNA is added, prompt: count the sequence differences again — assuming roughly comparable rates, fewer differences points to a more recent common ancestor, so where should this species attach?
When the tree reorganises, ask the learner to name the derived characters or DNA evidence that forced the move, so the revision is understood as evidence-driven, not arbitrary.
If a learner reads tips as 'more advanced', point out all tips are modern species that share ancestors at the nodes and do not descend from one another.
activities.rationale: Cladistics is fundamentally a constructive, data-driven inference: marking shared derived characters and counting molecular differences to assemble and revise a tree lets learners cause the reclassification rather than be told it. Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: an editable character/DNA-alignment matrix, a tree that redraws when molecular data are added, and a before/after showing birds moving inside the dinosaur clade when fossil skeletal characters are added. These are illustrative, not required.
sourceClaims: Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters (synapomorphies); phylogenetic trees are built from aligned molecular sequences and dated with the molecular clock (which has rate variation); birds are nested within theropod dinosaurs.
Anatomical similarities and DNA/molecular comparisons are used as evidence of evolutionary relationships and common ancestry.
learnerActions: Start with a small matrix of characters and DNA sequences for several species.
Mark which species share DERIVED characters and count sequence differences between pairs.
Group species by shared derived characters so a cladogram assembles, with common ancestors at the nodes and branch points as shared-ancestry hypotheses.

First build a tree using only overall appearance; then add molecular data and shared-derived-character data and observe which species move (e.g. DNA and mammalian features such as mammary glands move a dolphin placed beside sharks across to the mammals; fossil skeletal shared derived characters such as a wishbone and hollow bones place birds inside the dinosaurs, because no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs).
State in your own words why adding evidence changed the grouping.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is a testable hypothesis about shared ancestry that changes as new (especially molecular) evidence arrives; grouping is decided by shared derived characters and DNA, not by appearance.

activities.title: The convergence challenge: when resemblance lies
feedback: If a learner cites the shared fin/streamlined shape as evidence of relatedness, respond: that shape evolved independently for swimming (convergence); it was not inherited from a common ancestor, so it should not group them.

If a learner treats bird and bat wings as evidence of close relatedness, distinguish the two levels: the underlying forelimb bones are homologous across tetrapods, but flight capability (the 'wing' function) evolved independently, so function alone does not group them.
Affirm reasoning that invokes homologous, inherited features plus DNA to place the dolphin with mammals rather than with fish.
activities.rationale: Confronting look-alike but distantly related pairs directly targets the 'things that look alike are most closely related' misconception and teaches learners to distinguish analogy from homology.
sourceClaims: Convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages (misleading resemblance), and horizontal gene transfer, especially among microbes, makes the tree of life partly a web.
learnerActions: Examine a look-alike pair that are distantly related, e.g. dolphin vs shark/tuna body shape, and contrast this with homologous forelimbs — bird wing, bat wing, and a human arm (or whale flipper) are the same inherited tetrapod forelimb skeleton, even though flight in a bird and a bat evolved independently.
Decide whether the shared streamlined shape is inherited from a common ancestor or arose independently.
Check the grouping against DNA/molecular distance and name deep inherited (homologous) features the dolphin shares with mammals — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones.
Explain why a convergent trait is evidence AGAINST using it to group species.
activities.intendedInsight: Convergent evolution produces similar traits in distantly related lineages under similar pressures; shared derived homologies (characters inherited from a common ancestor), tested with DNA, are what arbitrate grouping.

activities.title: Dating nodes and the tree-becoming-web frontier
feedback: If a learner treats a molecular date as exact, prompt: rates vary, so the date is a best estimate with a range, not a fixed value.
If a learner says revising classifications means past scientists were wrong, reframe: schemes improve as new evidence (DNA, fossils) accumulates; revision is how evidence-based science works.
activities.rationale: Introducing molecular comparison concretely (more differences ≈ longer since common ancestor) with the explicit rate-variation caveat keeps trees framed as hypotheses, and horizontal gene transfer shows the genuine frontier of how life's history is shaped. Optional concrete controls: a molecular-clock slider showing an uncertainty band, and a toggle that draws horizontal-gene-transfer links.
sourceClaims: Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters (synapomorphies); phylogenetic trees are built from aligned molecular sequences and dated with the molecular clock (which has rate variation); birds are nested within theropod dinosaurs.
Convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages (misleading resemblance), and horizontal gene transfer, especially among microbes, makes the tree of life partly a web.
learnerActions: Use molecular distance to order nodes in time — more sequence differences roughly means longer since the common ancestor, assuming comparable rates.
Apply a molecular-clock estimate to date a node, and note that estimates carry an uncertainty band because mutation rates vary across lineages and genes.
Add cross-branch links representing horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) and describe how they turn a purely branching tree into a partial web.
Explain why classification schemes keep being redrawn without this meaning earlier scientists were simply 'wrong'.
activities.intendedInsight: Molecular data can both build and date trees, but dates are hypotheses with uncertainty; horizontal gene transfer means ancestry is not always a clean branching tree.

activities.title: Read a cladogram explicitly before building
feedback: If a learner says one living tip evolved from a neighbouring living tip, correct: all tips are modern; they share common ancestors back at the nodes.
If a learner reads the tree as a primitive-to-advanced ladder, re-point to the branching structure: it shows shared ancestry, not a ranking.
activities.rationale: Tree reading is a documented stumbling block, so explicit reading practice (including the common-ancestor and 'descends from a neighbour' errors) is valuable groundwork before or alongside tree-building. A static labelled cladogram supports reading but does not by itself let learners build or revise a tree.
learnerActions: On a labelled cladogram, identify which two species share the most recent common ancestor.

Point to a node (branch point) and state what it represents (a hypothesised common ancestor); point to a derived character marked on the branch leading to that node and state what it represents (a shared derived character supporting the group that descends from that node).

Given a sequence table, order several species by molecular distance from a chosen reference species, treating fewer differences as a hypothesis of closer relatedness, assuming roughly comparable rates.
Answer: do the species at the tips descend from one another, or from shared ancestors at the nodes?
activities.intendedInsight: Tree literacy — nodes as common ancestors, branching as shared-ancestry hypotheses, tips as modern species sharing ancestors rather than descending from each other.

activities.title: Discussion extension: why do textbooks keep redrawing the tree of life?
feedback: Push learners to ground opinions in specific evidence types (shared derived characters, DNA/molecular distance, fossils) rather than general assertion.
If a learner frames revision as scientists being unreliable, reframe revision as the normal response to new data.
activities.rationale: A role-based discussion can deepen the 'classification is revisable' and 'tree-vs-web' ideas, but it supplements rather than replaces the constructive building/reading of trees from data.
learnerActions: Discuss, in the role of a systematist, why classifications keep changing and what counts as good evidence for moving a group.
Argue whether the 'tree of life' is better described as a tree or a web, citing horizontal gene transfer.

Explain how you would check a surprising claim (e.g. that birds belong within dinosaurs) using shared derived characters in fossil skeletons (e.g. wishbone, hollow bones, feathers preserved in some theropod fossils). Note that DNA can test how birds relate to living groups (their closest living relatives are crocodilians), but no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is an ongoing, evidence-based scientific debate, not a fixed set of labels.

constraints: A static, tappable cladogram supports tree-reading (identifying nodes and most-recent-common-ancestor) but does not let learners build or revise a tree from data, which is the core constructive skill of cladistics; treat it as a scaffold.

Multiple-choice and sequence tasks (read-the-cladogram, order by molecular distance, identify convergent look-alikes) assess interpretation and catch the 'look-alike = related' and 'descends from a neighbour' errors, but they test interpretation rather than the constructive, revise-with-data skill; use them for assessment, not as the only teaching.
Group by shared DERIVED characters (derived homologies) and DNA, never by overall resemblance or shared lifestyle; convergent traits are evidence against grouping, not for it.
Distinguish levels when using wings: the tetrapod forelimb skeleton is homologous, but flight (bird vs bat wing function) evolved independently, so function alone is not grouping evidence.
Present molecular-clock dates with uncertainty: mutation rates vary across lineages and genes, so dates are estimates, not exact; molecular-distance ordering assumes roughly comparable rates.
Frame classification as a testable, revisable hypothesis; revision reflects new evidence, not past error.
A role-play conversation is an optional extension; the central skill is building and reading trees from data.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources carry verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels birds as 'crown Avemetatarsalia' in one field while elsewhere (correctly) describing birds as nested within theropod dinosaurs; Avemetatarsalia is a much broader clade than theropods. Activities use 'birds nested within theropod dinosaurs' and avoid the 'crown Avemetatarsalia' phrasing; a specialist should reconcile the exact clade name.

The source distinguishes convergent from parallel evolution in the description but gives little operational detail on parallel evolution; activities focus on convergence vs homology, which is the better-supported discriminator here. Parallel evolution could be added if a reliable worked example is available.

The original 3D artefact rationale asserted '3D offers no conceptual gain'; this has been treated as a narrow design note (the content is data-driven inference, not spatial) rather than a universal claim about what 3D can teach.

Molecular distance ordering (more differences ≈ longer since common ancestor) is a useful heuristic but assumes roughly comparable rates; it is stated with the rate-variation caveat in both the build and dating activities and should not be taught as exact.

The source used bird/bat/insect wings as a convergence example; the homology contrast here uses a distinct-taxa vertebrate forelimb set (bird wing/bat wing/human arm or whale flipper) to avoid the earlier redundancy of pairing 'bat wing' with 'mammal forelimb' (a bat is a mammal). A specialist should confirm the preferred example set and the wording that separates forelimb homology from independently evolved flight.

probeDeeper: The dolphin's fin and the tuna's fin do the same job. Does that make them closely related? How would you check?
Birds are classified as a group within the dinosaurs. What evidence would place them there, despite how different a sparrow looks from a T. rex?
Why do classification schemes keep changing — does that mean scientists were simply 'wrong' before?
The 'tree of life' is sometimes called a 'web'. What could make ancestry a web rather than a purely branching tree?
assess.correctAnswer: No — grouping should be by shared DERIVED characters inherited from a common ancestor (homologies), not by overall resemblance. The dolphin's streamlined shape is convergent evolution: it arose independently for swimming and was not inherited from a fish ancestor. Dolphins share deep inherited features with mice — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a common ancestor confirmed by DNA — so they group with mammals. Shared derived traits and DNA sequence data, not superficial similarity, decide the grouping, which is why the dolphin belongs with the mouse.

errorPatterns.pattern: Group organisms by how similar they look or how they live
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce homology versus analogy — group by shared derived characters from a common ancestor, tested with DNA, not by appearance.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — dolphins should go with sharks and tuna, because they look alike and both live in the sea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groups dolphin with fish, or bat with birds, on resemblance or shared lifestyle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convergent evolution means the species are closely related because they ended up similar
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convergence is independent evolution of similar traits in unrelated lineages — it is evidence AGAINST using that trait to group them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cites the shared streamlined shape as evidence that dolphin and tuna are related.

errorPatterns.pattern: A phylogenetic tree ranks species from primitive to advanced, or one living species evolved from another living one
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trees show shared ancestry and branching, not a ladder; living species share common ancestors, they don't descend from one another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads tree tips as 'more evolved', or says mammals evolved from living fish.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classification is fixed and just a matter of naming things
errorPatterns.nextMove: Present classification as a testable hypothesis about ancestry that changes as DNA and fossil data accumulate — e.g. birds nested within dinosaurs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists birds being classified within dinosaurs; treats groupings as arbitrary labels.

responseLevels.gap: Groups organisms by overall similarity or lifestyle (dolphin with fish), reads trees as primitive-to-advanced ladders, and treats classification as fixed naming.
responseLevels.full: Groups by shared derived characters from common ancestry (homology), tested with DNA/molecular data; distinguishes convergence/analogy from homology and explains why convergent traits mislead; reads trees as branching ancestry rather than a ladder; and treats classification as a data-revised hypothesis (birds within dinosaurs, tree-as-web via horizontal gene transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Knows the terms (shared characters, convergent evolution, phylogenetic tree) and can define them, but applies them inconsistently — still swayed by superficial resemblance in a new case, or unable to say why convergence argues against grouping — listing concepts without integrating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dolphin and a tuna both have sleek, streamlined bodies and fins and live in the sea — a tuna looks far more like a dolphin than a mouse does. So should dolphins be grouped with sharks and tuna (fish) rather than with mice (mammals)? How do scientists actually decide?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student using overall similarity groups the dolphin with the fish. A student using cladistic reasoning invokes shared derived/homologous characters and common ancestry (backed by DNA) and names the fish-like shape as convergence. Distinguishing homology from analogy is the discriminator.
